notes.heading: Introduction to Economic Zoology
points: Economic zoology deals with animals that are useful to humans
It includes animals used for food, agriculture, industry, and ecosystem services
Focus is on beneficial and commercially important animals
Helps in understanding sustainable use of animal resources
Important branch for biotechnology, agriculture, and fisheries

notes.heading: Corals – Importance
points: Corals are marine invertebrates forming coral reefs
They live in symbiosis with algae called zooxanthellae
Coral reefs are biodiversity hotspots
Protect coastlines from erosion and storms
Used in tourism and marine ecosystem balance

notes.heading: Earthworm – Importance
points: Earthworms are called ‘friends of farmers’
They improve soil fertility by aeration and mixing
Help in decomposition of organic matter
Increase nutrient availability in soil
Used in vermicomposting

notes.heading: Vermiculture
points: Vermiculture is the rearing of earthworms
Used for producing vermicompost (organic fertilizer)
Eco-friendly method of waste management
Improves soil structure and fertility
Reduces dependence on chemical fertilizers

notes.heading: Beneficial Insects
points: Insects that provide economic or ecological benefits
Bees: pollination and honey production
Silkworms: production of silk
Ladybird beetles: natural pest control
Important in agriculture and biodiversity

notes.heading: Prawns, Lobsters and Crabs
points: Belong to crustacean group of marine animals
Important source of seafood and protein
Prawn farming is a major aquaculture activity
Lobsters are high-value commercial seafood
Crabs are consumed widely and support fisheries economy

notes.heading: Pearl Oysters
points: Pearl oysters produce natural pearls
Pearls are formed as a protective response to irritants
Used in jewellery and luxury trade
Cultured pearl farming is widely practiced
Important part of marine aquaculture industry

notes.heading: Fishes – Economic Importance
points: Fish are a major source of protein for humans
Support inland and marine fisheries
Used in aquaculture (fish farming)
Provide fish oil and other industrial products
Important for livelihood in coastal regions

notes.heading: Guano
points: Guano is accumulated excreta of seabirds, bats, and seals
Rich in nitrogen, phosphate, and potassium
Used as a natural fertilizer
Highly effective in agriculture
Historically important export product in some countries

notes.heading: Aquarium
points: An aquarium is a tank for keeping aquatic organisms
Used for decoration, education, and research
Helps in studying aquatic life in controlled environment
Requires proper maintenance of water quality
Supports conservation awareness

notes.heading: Vivarium
points: A vivarium is an enclosed area for keeping animals/plants
Can simulate natural habitat conditions
Used for research and educational purposes
Includes terrariums (land) and aquariums (water)
Helps in studying behavior and ecology of organisms

name: Biology: Harmful Animals (Vectors, Poisonous Organisms, Fouling Organisms & Pests)

notes.heading: Introduction to Harmful Animals
points: Harmful animals are organisms that negatively affect human health, agriculture, or economy
They may spread diseases, damage crops, or contaminate environments
They include disease-causing organisms, vectors, pests, poisonous and fouling organisms
Understanding them is important for public health and agriculture management
Control measures are essential for disease prevention and economic protection

notes.heading: Disease-Causing Organisms (Pathogens)
points: Pathogens are organisms that cause diseases in humans, animals, and plants
They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and worms
Spread through air, water, food, and vectors
Examples: Plasmodium (malaria), Vibrio cholerae (cholera)
Control through hygiene, vaccination, and sanitation

notes.heading: Vectors – Overview
points: Vectors are organisms that transmit disease-causing pathogens
They do not necessarily cause disease themselves
Common vectors include mosquitoes, flies, ticks, and fleas
They spread diseases between humans, animals, or plants
Vector control is key in disease prevention

notes.heading: Examples of Disease Vectors
points: Mosquito – malaria, dengue, chikungunya
Housefly – typhoid, cholera
Tick – Lyme disease
Flea – plague
Sandfly – kala-azar

notes.heading: Poisonous Organisms
points: Poisonous organisms produce toxins harmful to humans or animals
Toxins can be injected or ingested
Examples include snakes, jellyfish, and scorpions
Venom is injected through bites or stings
Poisonous plants and fungi also exist

notes.heading: Examples of Poisonous Animals
points: Snake – neurotoxic or hemotoxic venom
Jellyfish – stinging cells (cnidocytes)
Scorpion – painful venomous sting
Pufferfish – contains tetrodotoxin
Spiders – some species are highly venomous

notes.heading: Fouling Organisms
points: Fouling organisms grow on submerged surfaces
They attach to ships, pipelines, and underwater structures
Examples include barnacles, algae, and mussels
Cause corrosion and reduce efficiency of machines
Marine fouling increases fuel consumption in ships

notes.heading: Impact of Fouling Organisms
points: Increase drag on ships, reducing speed
Damage underwater structures
Increase maintenance costs
Block pipelines and water systems
Affect marine industry efficiency

notes.heading: Pests – Overview
points: Pests are organisms that damage crops, livestock, or stored food
Includes insects, rodents, weeds, and fungi
Major threat to agriculture and food security
Controlled using pesticides and biological methods
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is widely used

notes.heading: Examples of Pests
points: Locusts – destroy large areas of crops
Termites – damage wooden structures and crops
Rodents – eat stored grains
Aphids – suck plant sap
Weeds – compete with crops for nutrients

notes.heading: Control Measures
points: Chemical control using pesticides and insecticides
Biological control using natural predators
Mechanical control like traps and barriers
Environmental management and sanitation
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) approach

notes.heading: Importance in UPSC
points: Frequently asked in Environment and Biology sections
Important for public health and agriculture-related questions
Relevant to disease control and vector management policies
Useful in disaster and epidemic management topics
Common in assertion-reason and match-the-following questions
